title: Language as probability
lede: Can you describe language well enough to predict it?
body: The story starts with a question from information theory rather than linguistics. In 1948 Claude Shannon treated English as a source of symbols and measured how predictable the next one was. For forty years afterwards, language models were counts: how often does this word follow those two? IBM used exactly that idea to translate text statistically, replacing hand-written grammar rules with probabilities learned from data.

Counting has a ceiling. Most sentences you will ever read have never been written before, so a model that only remembers sequences it has seen gives them zero probability. In 2003 Yoshua Bengio's group proposed learning a vector for every word, so that similar words share what the model knows about them. That single move, meaning as position in a learned space, is still inside every model today.
transition: The idea was right, but the computers were too slow to use it at scale. That changed a decade later.
